items.item: read your writes requires that if a process performs a write, and that same process performs a subsequent read, the read must observe the write's effects
read your writes does not apply to operations performed by different processes
monotonic reads ensures that if a process performs read r1, then r2, r2 cannot observe a state prior to the writes reflected in r1 — reads cannot go backwards
monotonic reads does not apply to operations performed by different processes, only reads by the same process
the primary and standby operate loosely coupled: the primary archives continuously while the standby recovers continuously, reading WAL from the primary
a server enters standby mode if a standby.signal file exists in the data directory at startup
a large difference between pg_last_wal_replay_lsn and pg_stat_wal_receiver's flushed_lsn indicates WAL is being received faster than it can be replayed
pg_stat_replication holds one row per WAL sender process, with statistics about replication to that sender's connected standby
the lag times in pg_stat_replication measure the time taken for recent WAL to be written, flushed and replayed, and for the sender to know about it
reported lag times are not predictions of catch-up time; a fully caught-up standby shows the time to write/flush/replay the most recent WAL location, not zero

items.item: Read-your-writes isn't broken by replication being slow — it's broken by the read happening to land on a node whose own replay position hasn't reached the write yet; a standby that is fast but still one commit behind breaks it just as surely as a slow one.

The LSN token this topic builds doesn't make the standby catch up faster — it only makes the read wait until the standby has already caught up to the one position that matters, which is why it is a correctness fix, not a performance one.

Monotonic reads and consistent-prefix reads both hold trivially on a single replica for the same structural reason: one WAL stream replayed in commit order can only ever move a replica's visible state forward, so neither anomaly has a mechanism to occur through.

A real monotonic-reads violation needs a session bounced between two replicas whose lag varies independently — if the second replica happens to be more caught up than the first at the moment of the second read, nothing is violated even though two different nodes answered.

pg_stat_replication's lag columns answer 'how long would a synchronous commit have waited', not 'how far behind is the standby right now' — which is why a fully caught-up idle standby still briefly shows its last real lag rather than zero.

Sticky routing fixes read-your-writes for free as long as a session never changes which node it talks to — the moment load balancing or a failover reroutes the session, the guarantee it was relying on silently disappears with it.

Primary fallback is the simplest fix precisely because it sidesteps the lag question entirely — it costs real primary capacity on every read that needs the guarantee, which is why it only scales for the minority of reads that actually need it.

Applying an LSN-token wait to a read that never needed read-your-writes doesn't make that read more correct — there was no guarantee being violated — it only makes it as slow as the primary, for a consistency property nobody was asking for.

This topic's own measured lag numbers (sub-millisecond, under 2,000 synchronous inserts) are themselves a result worth noticing: real replication lag under realistic load is often far smaller than the worst-case scenarios session guarantees are designed to survive.

items.item: Formal consistency models (linearizability, sequential consistency) describe what the whole system guarantees across every client; session guarantees describe what one client's own session can rely on — the two questions are related but answer different things, which is why this topic stops short of Chapter 14's own formal territory.
